query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount of high‐temperature stabilizing rare earth elements (specifically Y and Hf) into the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy will enhance its thermal stability, corrosion resistance, and mechanical performance (strength and ductility) under extreme temperature fluctuations, long‐term loading, room‐temperature creep, and corrosive environments.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 in a uniform, fine lamellar dual-phase (FCC/B2 or L12/B2) structure that shows lower than industrial requirements for strength and plasticity.
generation.intervention: Co‐doping with small additions of Yttrium (Y) and Hafnium (Hf) into the alloy (as part of the alloy composition or as a surface modification) without altering the overall lamellar morphology.
generation.conditions: Performance is targeted for fastener components operating under cyclic extreme temperature variations (up to ~700°C and rapid fluctuations), long-term mechanical loading that may induce creep at room temperature, and exposure to corrosive media (e.g., chloride-containing environments or molten salts).
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of the fine lamellar architecture with phase boundaries that become slightly enriched with Y and Hf, reinforcing both the FCC/L12 and B2 phases and increasing their interfacial stability.
generation.mechanism: The Y and Hf additions are expected to segregate to grain and phase boundaries, thereby inhibiting grain coarsening (improving thermal stability), retarding the nucleation and propagation of microcracks (enhancing ductility and damage tolerance), and promoting the formation of a more adherent, protective oxide layer under high temperature and corrosive conditions—thereby reducing oxide scale spallation and mitigating corrosion-induced degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Y/Hf-doped material will display higher yield and ultimate strength along with improved ductility and creep resistance at ambient and elevated temperatures, as well as improved corrosion resistance under severe conditions.
generation.baseline: The original AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic alloy in its fine lamellar state, which, while demonstrating an attractive composite microstructure, suffers from insufficient mechanical performance and stability under extreme operating environments.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective within operating temperatures up to about 700°C, under long-term static and cyclic mechanical load, in room-temperature creep conditions, and in corrosive environments similar to chloride or molten salt media. Its benefits may diminish if dopant levels are too high or if exposure significantly exceeds these conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The optimum concentrations of Y and Hf that balance enhanced stability against possible embrittlement, and the long-term performance under cyclic thermo-mechanical fatigue remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloys – one as the baseline and one doped with optimized small amounts of Y and Hf. Fabricate specimens with identical fine lamellar microstructures using the same casting and thermo-mechanical processing routes. Subject both sets of samples to accelerated aging and thermal cycling (simulating extreme temperature fluctuations), long-term mechanical loading (including creep tests at room temperature), and corrosive attack in chloride-containing or molten salt environments.
measurements: Mechanical properties (yield strength, ultimate tensile/compressive strength, ductility, and creep rate) at room and elevated temperatures.
Microstructural stability (grain size, phase boundary integrity) post thermal cycling and long-term load.
Corrosion metrics (oxide scale adhesion, spallation area, weight loss or corrosion current density).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y/Hf-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant (e.g., >15%) improvement in the key performance metrics—mechanical strength, ductility, creep resistance, and corrosion resistance—over the baseline alloy under simulated service conditions, or if the doped alloy exhibits adverse effects (such as increased brittleness or early failure), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. 1.
